passage: Parul was halfway through her vada pav in the canteen when her phone started buzzing nonstop. The class group. Harish and Sameer were still going at it over yesterday's comment about the cricket match, but now thirty people were watching. Someone posted a screenshot of Sameer's old message with a clown face on it. Someone else forwarded it to the other section's group. Every reply got a row of reactions within seconds. Parul looked across the canteen. Harish was hunched over his phone, jaw tight, typing and deleting. Sameer sat with his friends, reading replies aloud to cheers. Neither of them could stop now, Parul thought. Whoever went quiet first would be the one who lost, in front of everyone.

qa.q: Where was Parul when her phone started buzzing?
qa.a: She was in the canteen, halfway through her vada pav.

qa.q: What does Parul think is keeping Harish and Sameer from stopping?
qa.a: She thinks both of them feel trapped by the watching crowd: whoever goes quiet first will look like the loser in front of everyone.

qa.q: What could Parul do as an onlooker to take some fuel out of the fight?
qa.a: She could stop reacting and forwarding, post "Let them sort it offline", or quietly message one of them.

qa.q: What is it like for Harish, typing and deleting with thirty people watching?
qa.a: He seems tense and trapped, with every word judged in public, so a calm reply feels risky.

grounding: Shows a classmate watching reactions and screenshots turn a quarrel into a show where backing down feels like losing in public.

passage:
"Simran, your dinner's getting cold."
"One minute, Maria di. Look, forty-two people have seen it."
Maria sat beside her sister on the sofa. The class chat was scrolling by itself. "Who's Khushi?"
"The one who started it. She said my project was copied, and now everyone's sending popcorn emojis."
"So say sorry for your snappy reply and leave it?"
"Are you mad? If I back down now, the whole school will think she's right."
The phone buzzed. Another screenshot. Simran's thumb was already moving.
"Wait," Maria said. "Would you still be fighting if nobody was watching?"
Simran paused. "...Probably not."
"Then who is this fight for?"
Simran looked at the screen, at the count going up, and put the phone face down on the cushion.

qa.q: How many people had seen it, according to Simran?
qa.a: Forty-two people had seen it.

qa.q: Why does Simran refuse to back down at first?
qa.a: She fears the whole school will think Khushi is right, so her reputation feels at stake with everyone watching.

qa.q: What question helps Simran step back, and why?
qa.a: Maria asks whether she would still fight if nobody was watching, which helps her see the audience is driving it.

qa.q: How might Khushi be feeling with the same crowd watching her?
qa.a: Khushi is probably under the same pressure, feeling she cannot back down either without losing face.

grounding: Shows an older sister noticing how an audience of reactions turns a quarrel into a show that neither teen can leave without losing face.

passage:
I still think about the Sunday the class group turned into a stage.
Anand and Pratik started arguing about who let the team down in the quiz. Normal stuff. But then people started reacting. Popcorn emojis. Someone screenshot Pratik's worst line and posted it in the girls' chat too. Somebody added a poll: "Who won?"
I watched from my bed, thumb hovering. I could see Anand's messages getting longer and angrier, like he couldn't stop now because forty people were watching. Pratik too.
I almost sent a laughing emoji like everyone else. Then I saw Anand's last line, "fine, I'm done," and I felt a little sick. I didn't send anything. I'm Disha, and I think staying quiet was only half of what I should have done.

qa.q: What did someone add to the group while the argument was going on?
qa.a: A poll asking "Who won?"

qa.q: What was Disha feeling while watching the argument grow?
qa.a: Disha felt uneasy and a little sick, especially after Anand's "fine, I'm done" line, sensing the show was hurting real people.

qa.q: What turning point could an onlooker like Disha offer at this stage?
qa.a: Disha could privately message Anand or Pratik to check on them, or post something that lowers the heat, instead of feeding the audience.

qa.q: What was Anand experiencing with forty people watching?
qa.a: He felt trapped defending his reputation; backing down in front of everyone felt like a public loss, so he kept going until he gave up.

grounding: An onlooker watches a class chat argument turn into a show with emojis, screenshots and a poll, and sees both teens unable to back down.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 9B

On Monday three students came to me with phones. Over the weekend Dilnaz and Simran had argued in the class chat about a missed group-project deadline. By Sunday night the messages had screenshots, a sticker of a boxing ring, and dozens of reactions. Other students were adding "round 2" and clapping emojis.
In class both girls sat stiffly apart. When I asked Dilnaz quietly, she said, "If I say sorry now, everyone will say I lost."
I spoke to each girl alone, then asked the class to take the thread down. I told the class that we don't turn a friend's fight into a show. I'll meet both girls together on Wednesday.

qa.q: What did the class teacher ask the class to do?
qa.a: To take the thread down.

qa.q: What was the teacher feeling when three students came with phones?
qa.a: The teacher was concerned and uneasy, seeing that a private disagreement had become a public show that both girls felt trapped in.

qa.q: What turning point did the teacher use at this stage?
qa.a: Speaking to each girl alone, away from the audience, and asking the class to remove the thread took away the pressure to keep performing.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz experiencing when she spoke to the teacher?
qa.a: She felt trapped by the audience; saying sorry felt like a public loss, even if part of her wanted to stop.

grounding: A teacher notices a chat quarrel turning into a show with emojis and screenshots, where both girls fear backing down would mean losing publicly.

passage:
Diary, late Friday

Okay so today was a mess and I was part of it.
Maria and Kiran started fighting in the tuition chat about who copied whose notes. At first it was just them. Then Sid posted a screenshot from last month. Then the reactions started, 😮 and 👀, and someone wrote "FIGHT FIGHT FIGHT."
I sent a 👀 too. Just one. It felt harmless.
But I could see Maria's messages getting sharper, like she was performing for us, not talking to Kiran. And Kiran wouldn't back down either, not with twenty people reading.
It's 11 pm. I just texted Maria privately: "You okay? Want to call?" No reply yet. — Rajni

qa.q: What reaction did Rajni send in the tuition chat?
qa.a: Rajni sent a 👀 too, just one, in the tuition chat.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling by the end of the day?
qa.a: Rajni felt guilty and uneasy for adding to the audience, and worried enough about Maria to text privately.

qa.q: What turning point did Rajni try at this stage?
qa.a: Rajni stepped away from the audience and texted Maria privately to check in, which gives Maria a way out without losing face in public.

qa.q: What might Maria be experiencing with twenty people reading?
qa.a: She likely feels pressured to keep winning for the audience, and backing down now would feel like a public loss.

grounding: A student watching a chat quarrel notices how reactions and screenshots turn it into a show, then quietly steps away from the audience.
